Anya runs 12 km at x km/h and next day walks 10 km at (x−4) km/h. (a) Running time. [1] (b) Walking time. [1] (c) Show the condition that walking is 1 hour longer simplifies to x²−2x−48=0. [4] (d) Solve by factorisation. [3] (e) Find running time. [1]
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: Running=12/x; walking=10/(x−4). Set 10/(x−4)−12/x=1; clearing denominators gives x²−2x−48=0. Factor: (x+6)(x−8)=0, so x=−6 or 8; valid speed x=8. Running time=12/8=1.5 h.

blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: The graph gives (a,b)=(1,2). Gradient=(2−11)/(1+2)=−3. Using (1,2), c=5, so y=5−3x.

The coordinate graph shows the unshaded quadrilateral region R with vertices (1, 1), (5, 5), (6, 5), and (6, 1). The boundaries y = x and x = 6 are dashed, while y = 1 and y = 5 are solid. Find the inequalities that define the unshaded region R.
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: The region is below the dashed line y = x, so y < x. It lies to the left of the dashed line x = 6, so x < 6. The solid horizontal boundaries are included: y ≥ 1 and y ≤ 5. Therefore the inequalities are y < x, x < 6, 1 ≤ y ≤ 5.

Solve the simultaneous equations, showing all working: (3x/2) + 5y = 5; 4x − 3y = 46.
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: Multiply the first equation by 2: 3x + 10y = 10. Multiply the second equation by 3: 12x − 9y = 138. Eliminate y by multiplying the first result by 9 and the second by 10: 27x + 90y = 90 and 120x − 90y = 1380. Adding gives 147x = 1470, so x = 10. Substitute into 4x − 3y = 46: 40 − 3y = 46, hence y = −2.

blindEvidence.accessibleText: [Maximum mark: 15] Consider the function f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d, where x ∈ ℝ and where a, b, c and d are real constants. The graph of f has a point of inflexion at (−2, −2c + d + 24). (a) Show that a = 3/2 and b = 9. [6] It is given that the tangents to the graph of f at x = −3 and x = k are horizontal. (b) (i) Show that c = 27/2. (ii) Find the value of k. (iii) State whether f has a local maximum or a local minimum at x = k, justifying your answer. [7] The graph of f intersects the y-axis at the point P. (c) Show that the tangent to the graph of f at x = −3 passes through P. [2]
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: Write f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d. Since the inflection point has x-coordinate −2, f''(−2)=0: −12a+2b=0, so b=6a. Its y-coordinate condition gives f(−2)=−2c+d+24. But f(−2)=−8a+4b−2c+d=16a−2c+d, hence 16a=24 and a=3/2, b=9. (b)(i) The horizontal tangent at x=−3 gives f'(−3)=0. Since f'(x)=3ax^2+2bx+c, 27a−6b+c=0, so c=27/2. (ii) f'(x)=(9/2)x^2+18x+27/2=(9/2)(x+3)(x+1), so the other horizontal tangent is at k=−1. (iii) f''(x)=9x+18, so f''(−1)=9>0; therefore f has a local minimum at x=−1. (c) The y-intercept is P=(0,d). At x=−3, f(−3)=d, and f'(−3)=0, so the tangent there is horizontal, hence its equation is y=d and it passes through P.

blindEvidence.accessibleText: [Maximum mark: 25] This question asks you to explore curves in the complex plane defined by r = a + b sin θ, where a and b are real constants. A complex number z can be represented by a point in the complex plane whose position is determined by the modulus, r, and the argument, θ, of z. The set of points which satisfy a given relationship between r and θ form a curve in the complex plane. Consider a family of curves defined by r = a + b sin θ, where a and b are real constants. First consider the case where a = 4 and b = 0 so that r = 4. The curve defined by r = 4 is the set of points in the complex plane which represent complex numbers with a modulus of 4. (a) Suppose that z is a complex number such that r = 4. Find all possible values of z such that (i) z is purely real; [1] (ii) z is purely imaginary; [1] (iii) the argument of z is π/4. [1] (b) Sketch the curve defined by r = 4 on an Argand diagram, showing clearly the values of the intercepts with the real and imaginary axes. [2] Now consider the case where a = 0 and b = 4 so that r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. (c) Suppose that z is a complex number such that r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. (i) Write down the greatest possible value of r. [1] (ii) For this value of r, find z. [2] (d) Use the identities x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ to show that the points on the curve defined by r = 4 sin θ lie on the curve x² + (y − 2)² = 4, where x = Re(z) and y = Im(z). [4] The question continues on the following page. (e) Consider the curve x² + (y − 2)² = 4. (i) Find an expression for dy/dx in terms of x and y. [3] (ii) Hence or otherwise, find the values of x for which the gradient of the curve is undefined. [2] (f) The curve defined by r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, is a circle. Sketch this curve on an Argand diagram, showing clearly the values of any intercepts with the real and imaginary axes. [1] Finally, consider the case where a = 4 and b = 4. The curve defined by r = 4 + 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, is shown on the following Argand diagram. The curve has a horizontal tangent at point A, point B and point C. The real parts of the numbers represented by A, B and C are negative, positive and zero, respectively. Diagram description: an Argand diagram with horizontal Re axis and vertical Im axis; the limacon r = 4 + 4 sin θ is drawn, passing through the origin, with a large upper loop reaching Im = 8 and extending from Re = −4 to Re = 4, and a small lower loop reaching approximately Im = −2; point A is on the lower loop at negative real part, point B is on the lower loop at positive real part, and point C is on the positive imaginary axis at Im = 8. (g) Use the identities x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ to show that the gradient of the curve at the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) is given by dy/dx = cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ)/(1 − sin θ − 2 sin² θ). [5] (h) Hence, find the value of θ which corresponds to the point A. [2]
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText:
(a) (i) For r = 4, a purely real z has argument 0 or π, so z = 4e⁰ = 4 or z = 4eⁱπ = −4. Thus z = ±4.
(ii) A purely imaginary point on |z| = 4 has argument π/2 or 3π/2, so z = 4i or z = −4i. Thus z = ±4i.
(iii) If arg(z) = π/4, then z = 4(cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4)) = 4(√2/2 + i√2/2) = 2√2 + 2√2i.
(b) The locus r = 4 is the circle |z| = 4, centred at the origin with radius 4. Its intercepts are (4, 0), (−4, 0), (0, 4) and (0, −4); sketch this circle on an Argand diagram.
(c) (i) For r = 4 sin θ and 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, the greatest possible value of sin θ is 1, attained at θ = π/2. Hence r_max = 4.
(ii) At θ = π/2, z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = 4(0 + i) = 4i.
(d) With x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, r = 4 sin θ gives r² = 4r sin θ = 4y. Since r² = x² + y², x² + y² = 4y, so x² + (y − 2)² = 4. This is the circle centred at (0, 2) with radius 2.
(e) (i) Differentiate x² + (y − 2)² = 4 implicitly: 2x + 2(y − 2) dy/dx = 0. Therefore dy/dx = −x/(y − 2).
(ii) The gradient is undefined when y − 2 = 0, so y = 2. Substitution into x² + (y − 2)² = 4 gives x² = 4, hence x = ±2.
(f) The locus r = 4 sin θ is the circle x² + (y − 2)² = 4, centred at (0, 2) with radius 2. Its real-axis intercept is (0, 0); its imaginary-axis intercepts are (0, 0) and (0, 4). Sketch this circle on the Argand diagram.
(g) For r = 4 + 4 sin θ, x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. Since dr/dθ = 4 cos θ, dx/dθ = (dr/dθ)cos θ − r sin θ = 4(1 − sin θ − 2 sin²θ), while dy/dθ = (dr/dθ)sin θ + r cos θ = 4 cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ). Therefore, wherever dx/dθ ≠ 0, dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ) = cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ)/(1 − sin θ − 2 sin²θ).
(h) At A the tangent is horizontal, so dy/dx = 0. From the expression in (g), cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ) = 0. Point A is in the third quadrant and is not the top point, so cos θ ≠ 0 and 1 + 2 sin θ = 0. Thus sin θ = −1/2; in the third quadrant, θ = 7π/6.

Let f(x) = (x² + 3)⁷. Find the term in x⁵ in the expansion of the derivative, f′(x).
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: f′(x)=14x(x²+3)⁶. To obtain x⁵, choose the x⁴ term from (x²+3)⁶: C(6,2)x⁴3⁴=15·81x⁴. Multiplying by 14x gives 17010x⁵.

6. [Maximum mark: 6]

The binomial expansion of (1 + kx)ⁿ is given by 1 + 12x + 28k²x² + … + kⁿxⁿ, where n ∈ ℤ⁺ and k ∈ ℚ.

Find the value of n and the value of k.
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: From C(n,2)k² = 28k², n(n − 1)/2 = 28, so n(n − 1) = 56 and n = 8. The x coefficient gives nk = 12, so k = 3/2.

7. [Maximum mark: 16]

Graphs of f and g are shown. f is linear with x-intercept (6, 0) and y-intercept (0, 12). g has x-intercepts (−2, 0), (6, 0) and y-intercept (0, 12).

[Diagram: a descending line through (0, 12) and (6, 0), and a downward parabola through all three stated intercepts; the parabola is above the line between x=0 and x=6.]

(a) Write f(x)=mx+c. [2]

g(x)=−x²+bx+12.

(b) Find b. [3]

(c) Show that the enclosed area is ∫₀⁶(−x² + 6x) dx. [2]

(d) Hence find the area. [4]

At P on g, the tangent is parallel to f.

(e) Find P. [5]
blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: (a) Slope=−2, so f(x)=−2x + 12. (b) Substitution of (6,0) gives b=4. (c) g−f=−x² + 6x, so area=∫₀⁶(−x² + 6x) dx. (d) Integrating gives 36 square units. (e) g′(x)=−2x+4; equate to −2 and substitute in g, giving P=(3, 15).

blindEvidence.independentSolutionText: (a) Regression gives a=−0.454,b=6.14. (b) ln y=5.56484, so y=261. (c) ln y=lnk+nlnx, hence n=−0.454 and k=e^6.14210=465.
